“It is so hard,” the man sitting across from me said. “We’ve been married for nearly fifty years, but I never expected anything like this.”

“What is going on?” I asked Al, sympathetically.

“It’s Lisa,” he said. “You know her memory has been slipping for a little while. Well, we went to the neurologist like you told us to, and they ordered a whole bunch of tests and a brain scan of some sort. Then, they told her she had dementia.”

“I thought that was what was going on,” I replied.

“I know you told us that,” Al said. “Well, there are times she doesn’t recognize me. She looks at me blankly like she is wondering what crazy stranger has gotten into her house.”

“That’s got to be hard,” I said.

“The only thing I’ve found that brings her back to herself is to go outside and call her on her cell phone. I tell her to come out to the garage, I’ve got something to show her. Somehow when I do that, it brings her back to the present and lets her know who I am – for a little bit, anyway.”

We moved on to talking about other things, but I could tell that Al’s heart was breaking. His wife of 48 years looked the same as ever on the outside and yet, she was a completely different person.

I’d like to explore some of the challenges in dealing with dementia.

Dementia in the Bible

Ecclesiastes 12:1-7 gives a somewhat dismal view of the aging process. “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them; While the sun, or the light, or the moon, or the stars, be not darkened, nor the clouds return after the rain: In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those that look out of the windows be darkened, And the doors shall be shut in the streets, when the sound of the grinding is low, and he shall rise up at the voice of the bird, and all the daughters of musick shall be brought low; Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets: Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern. Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.”

In this passage, the poetic description seems to speak of loss of teeth, loss of hearing, unsteady gait, and general frailty. It is hard to say if any of these images speak of memory loss. What is certain is that the passage begins with a command: “Remember!”

This is not the only place in Scripture where humans are commanded to remember. Over and over, we are told to remember God. We are to make certain that we instruct our children about Him. “And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up” (Deuteronomy 6:7).

The time may come when we are not able to remember anymore. The most important thing – even as we think about the subject of dementia is that we remember the One who made us and follow Him with all our hearts.

What Dementia is

Dementia is any illness that causes a loss of memory, reasoning, and social functioning. Most people think mostly of the loss of memory. I suppose this is because early in the illness other people notice things like difficulty finding words and frequent repetition of stories.

Social functioning is often maintained until late in the illness. If you ask someone with mild dementia if they know today’s date, they will likely answer, “Oh, you know, I stopped paying attention to things like that when I retired.”

The most common cause of dementia is Alzheimer’s dementia – at least 70 percent of people who have progressive memory loss have Alzheimer’s dementia. Alzheimer’s seems to be related to proteins called amyloid, which get deposited in the brain and prevent nerve cells from communicating with each other.

Other causes are vascular dementia, where blockages in the blood vessels in the brain cause the death of nerve cells. Lewy Body Dementia is a sort of memory loss that is associated with Parkinson’s Disease. Approximately eighty percent of people with Parkinson’s Disease will eventually develop dementia.

Diagnosing Dementia

If family members suspect someone is developing memory loss, the best thing is to bring them to their primary care provider for an evaluation. Along with doing a physical exam, the doctor will typically do things like have the patient draw a clock and do a mini mental status exam, which asks the patient to answer a lot of simple questions and do some short-term recall of items.

Blood tests including a thyroid and Vitamin B12 level would be done. A brain scan or ultrasound of the neck arteries might be done as well.

The goal is to identify areas that can be treated and take care of those.

Eliminate Medications

Many medications increase the risk of memory issues. As people get older, trying to avoid these medications is helpful to prevent the development of dementia.

Anticholinergic medications are probably the biggest culprit that I encounter. The most common of these medications are older antihistamines like diphenhydramine (used as either a sleep aid or allergy pill) and doxylamine (used as a sleep aid). In one study, patients who took an anticholinergic medication for the equivalent of three years had a significantly higher risk of dementia than patients who took these sorts of medications for less than three months.1 Older depression medications can also fall into this category.

Anxiety medications, called benzodiazepines, have also been associated with memory issues. Studies indicate that patients who take these medications have a higher risk of developing dementia than patients who do not take them.2

Seizure medications may make thinking ability worse as well. Having a seizure disorder seems to increase the risk of dementia, but certain older medications like valproate and gabapentin seem to make it harder for older people to think clearly, and shifting to lower-risk seizure medications is in order (if possible) for older people.

There are times when someone needs to take medication, but as patients get older, it is important to think about the risks of those medications. There is a list of medications that are wisest to avoid for patients over 65 years of age, called the Beers List. Substituting similar medications with fewer side effects or using lower doses is recommended.3

Medical Treatments

The first rule when dealing with dementia is to make certain that all of the metabolic things are in as good control as possible. So, if someone has diabetes, it is best to make certain that their sugar is in as good control as possible. If someone has high blood pressure, make certain that it is well-regulated (this is particularly true if someone has vascular dementia).

There are several different classes of medications that are approved for treating dementia. One group is the cholinesterase inhibitors. These medications raise the level of a chemical called acetylcholine in the brain and peripheral nervous system. These medications are certainly not miracle drugs and at best they seem to slow the progression of memory loss and do not really restore previous brain function.

The other medication is called memantine. It works by targeting the glutamate receptor in the brain. Just as with the cholinesterase inhibitors, the effects are not huge and the end result only slows the memory loss.

Both of these medications are generic, and it is reasonable to try them and see how someone responds to them.

One last medication to mention is called lecanemab. It is an IV infusion that targets amyloid, a kind of protein that develops in the brain of people with Alzheimer’s dementia. The medication seems to work quite well at clearing amyloid from patient’s brains. This medication is very expensive ($26,500 per year)and it has been linked to an increase in strokes. In the studies, dementia symptoms were only slowed by about 30 percent compared with a placebo.

There are no other medications currently approved to treat dementia.

Non-medication Therapies

There are several things that people can do to help slow the progression of dementia. These can be helpful for people who have a strong family history of dementia and want to prevent its onset.

Cardiovascular exercise is very important. Doctors mention exercise in relation to nearly every chronic illness because it has been shown to work. In the case of dementia, people who exercise regularly have about 30 percent decreased risk of developing the disease. Regular exercise seems to slow the progression of dementia.4

Doing puzzles that require mental activity, like Sudoku or crossword puzzles seems to help slow the progression of memory loss and may also reduce the chance of developing dementia.

Lastly, it is helpful to learn something new. People who learn a new skill or focus on learning a new language help their memories quite a bit. A study compared older people who learned a new skill with people who went to social events.

The point seems to be that our brains need to be pushed to create new pathways or they will tend to break down.5

Caring For Someone with Dementia

Caring for someone with dementia is challenging in a number of ways. It is often difficult to know how much independence to allow the person. There have been many books written on this subject, but there are a few things that are worth mentioning.

It is important to avoid dangerous things. The two most dangerous things for someone with faulty memory are driving and cooking. Both of these seem commonplace, and the person may seem to be doing fine, but they can become a problem very quickly.

The danger of driving a car or a buggy is twofold. First, some people freeze at certain points, not remembering how to do a particular skill. This can be a problem, not only for them but also for others on the road.

Second, older people can start off on short journeys to a local store or restaurant and end up getting lost. I have had patients who ended up driving around for hours trying to find their way home when they got confused driving to town.

Cooking, of course, really comes down to a question of remembering to set timers and take things off the stove or out of the oven at the appropriate time.

Many times, people who have dementia do not realize how much their abilities have slipped and resist the idea that they need to give up the car keys. Maybe it simply comes down to a loss of independence, but it is hard to face the fact that you are no longer safe behind the wheel.

Try to keep things the same within the room and the home. Even small changes in room arrangement can be enough to upset the situation. Taking someone out of their home – for instance, admitting them to the hospital often makes things a lot worse. Suddenly, confusion that only seemed mild before is now extremely high.

If there is a fruit of the spirit that is key for dealing with someone with dementia, it is patience. None of us has as much patience as we need, as dementia spreads that patience awfully thin.

People with dementia often act like children on a long trip. They ask over and over when they are going home. They wonder where dead relatives are or why the children aren’t home yet. No amount of explanation helps, because only a minute or two after they ask the question, they have forgotten the answer and are asking again.

Their skills often wax and wane. One day, they can button their shirt, and the next day, that skill seems to have flown out the window. It is easy to believe that they aren’t “trying hard” and that they could do more if they would only make the effort.

Unfortunately, the fact that someone with dementia could do something yesterday doesn’t mean that they can remember how to do it today. Getting upset with them only makes these things worse as it adds anxiety to a person who already lacks the memory of how to do a skill.

As much as possible, answer the person gently even if it is the fifty-third time that you have answered the same question. Use distractions as well. If there is an activity that they can still do, such as sewing or jigsaw puzzles (even children’s puzzles with really big pieces), get them to do it. Late in the illness, letting them look at books with pretty pictures or sometimes even giving them a baby doll to hold can help settle them and distract them from their anxieties of the moment.

Get Others to Help

It is easy to become frustrated. Trying to provide all of the care needed by yourself is not a long-term solution. Dementia care is a marathon and not a sprint. Many people live for years after the diagnosis, and even though their physical body remains relatively strong, they require more and more care.

One of the blessings of having family connections and church communities is that we have people who are available to provide assistance.

Having family members or friends step in to give you some respite is key to not becoming seriously burned out or even angry with someone that you care about. It is best to take some time away periodically before you are mentally depleted. You may think you are doing fairly well, but all of us have a tendency to get weary in well doing if we never get a break.

Conclusion

I wish there were more medical solutions for dementia. Perhaps more will come later. For now, medications are quite limited.

The key is to put the fruit of the Spirit into practice. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law” (Galatians 5:22-23).

Even on the most frustrating days, people who are dealing with severe memory loss need love, gentleness, and patience from their family members. It is only through the Holy Spirit’s power that we can provide the care that is needed for someone whose body is strong, but who no longer even recognizes you.

“Det är så svårt,” sa mannen som satt mitt emot mig. “Vi har varit gifta i nästan femtio år, men jag väntade mig aldrig något liknande.”

“Vad händer?” frågade jag Al medlidsamt.

“Det är Lisa,” sa han. “Du vet att hennes minne har blivit sämre ett tag. Vi gick till neurolog som du sade åt oss att göra, och de beställde en massa tester och någon sorts hjärnskanning. Sedan sa de att hon hade demens.”

“Jag trodde att det var vad som pågick,” svarade jag.

“Jag vet att du sa det,” sa Al. “Det finns tillfällen då hon inte känner igen mig. Hon tittar på mig tomt som om hon undrar vilken galen främling som kommit in i hennes hus.”

“Det måste ju vara svårt,” sa jag.

“Det enda jag har funnit som får henne att komma tillbaka till sig själv är att gå ut och ropa på henne på hennes mobil. Jag säger åt henne att komma ut till garaget, jag har något att visa henne. På något sätt, när jag gör det, får det henne att återvända till nuet och veta vem jag är – åtminstone en liten stund.”

Vi gick vidare och pratade om andra saker, men jag kunde se att Als hjärta brast. Hans fru på 48 år såg likadan ut som alltid utvändigt och ändå var hon en helt annan person.

Jag vill gärna ta upp några av utmaningarna i att hantera demens.

Demens i Bibeln

Predikaren 12:1-7 ger en något dyster bild av åldrandeprocessen. “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them; While the sun, or the light, or the moon, or the stars, be not darkened, nor the clouds return after the rain: In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those that look out of the windows be darkened, And the doors shall be shut in the streets, when the sound of the grinding is low, and he shall rise up at the voice of the bird, and all the daughters of musick shall be brought low; Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets: Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern. Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.”

I denna passage talar den poetiska beskrivningen om tandsförlust, hörselförlust, ostadig gång och allmän svaghet. Det är svårt att säga om någon av dessa bilder handlar om minnesförlust. Det som är säkert är att avsnittet börjar med en befallning: “Remember!”

Detta är inte det enda stället i Skriften där människor befallas att minnas. Om och om igen uppmanas vi att komma ihåg Gud. Vi ska försäkra oss om att undervisa våra barn om Honom. “And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up” (Deuteronomy 6:7).

Tiden kan komma då vi inte längre kan minnas. Det viktigaste – även när vi tänker på ämnet demens – är att vi minns Den som skapade oss och följer Honom av hela vårt hjärta.

Vad demens är

Demens är vilken sjukdom som helst som orsakar förlust av minne, resonemang och social funktion. De flesta tänker mest på minnesförlusten. Jag antar att det är för att andra tidigt märker svårigheter att hitta ord och frekvent upprepning av berättelser.

Social funktion bibehålls ofta tills sent i sjukdomen. Om du frågar någon med mild demens om de vet dagens datum kommer de sannolikt svara: “Åh, du vet, jag slutade lägga märke till sådant när jag gick i pension.”

Den vanligaste orsaken till demens är Alzheimers demens – åtminstone 70 procent av personer med progressiv minnesförlust har Alzheimers demens. Alzheimer tycks vara relaterat till proteiner som kallas amyloid, vilka deponeras i hjärnan och förhindrar nervceller från att kommunicera med varandra.

Andra orsaker är vaskulär demens, där tilltäppningar i hjärnans blodkärl orsakar nervcellers död. Lewy body-demens är en sorts minnesförlust som är kopplad till Parkinsons sjukdom. Ungefär åttio procent av personer med Parkinsons sjukdom utvecklar så småningom demens.

Att diagnostisera demens

Om familjemedlemmar misstänker att någon utvecklar minnesproblem är det bästa att ta personen till sin primärvårdsläkare för en utredning. Förutom att göra en fysisk undersökning gör läkaren vanligtvis saker som att låta patienten rita en klocka och göra ett mini mental status-test, som ber patienten svara på många enkla frågor och göra några korttidsminnesuppgifter.

Blodprov inklusive sköldkörtel- och vitamin B12-nivåer tas också. En hjärnskanning eller ultraljud av halsartärerna kan också göras.

Målet är att identifiera områden som kan behandlas och ta hand om dem.

Uteslut läkemedel

Många läkemedel ökar risken för minnesproblem. När människor blir äldre är det hjälpsamt att undvika dessa läkemedel för att förebygga utveckling av demens.

Antikolinerga läkemedel är förmodligen den största boven som jag stöter på. De vanligaste av dessa läkemedel är äldre antihistaminer som diphenhydramin (använt som sömnmedel eller allergitablett) och doxylamin (använt som sömnmedel). I en studie hade patienter som tog ett antikolinergt läkemedel motsvarande tre års användning en avsevärt högre risk för demens än patienter som tog sådana läkemedel i mindre än tre månader.1 Äldre läkemedel mot depression kan också falla in i denna kategori.

Ångestdämpande läkemedel, så kallade bensodiazepiner, har också kopplats till minnesproblem. Studier visar att patienter som tar dessa läkemedel har en högre risk att utveckla demens än patienter som inte tar dem.2

Anfallsmedicin kan också göra tänkandet sämre. Att ha en anfallssjukdom verkar öka risken för demens, men vissa äldre läkemedel som valproat och gabapentin verkar göra det svårare för äldre att tänka klart, och att byta till anfallsmediciner med lägre risk är lämpligt (om möjligt) för äldre.

Det finns tillfällen då någon behöver ta läkemedel, men när patienter blir äldre är det viktigt att tänka på riskerna med dessa läkemedel. Det finns en lista över läkemedel som är klokast att undvika för patienter över 65 år, kallad Beers-listan. Att ersätta med liknande läkemedel med färre biverkningar eller använda lägre doser rekommenderas.3

Medicinska behandlingar

Den första regeln vid hantering av demens är att säkerställa att alla metabola faktorer är så välkontrollerade som möjligt. Så om någon har diabetes är det bäst att se till att blodsockret är så välkontrollerat som möjligt. Om någon har högt blodtryck, se till att det är välreglerat (detta är särskilt viktigt vid vaskulär demens).

Det finns flera olika klasser av läkemedel som är godkända för att behandla demens. En grupp är kolinesterashämmare. Dessa läkemedel höjer nivån av en kemikalie som kallas acetylkolin i hjärnan och det perifera nervsystemet. Dessa läkemedel är absolut inga mirakelmedel och i bästa fall verkar de bromsa utvecklingen av minnesförlust och återställer inte tidigare hjärnfunktion.

Det andra läkemedlet kallas memantin. Det verkar genom att rikta in sig på glutamatreceptorn i hjärnan. Liksom med kolinesterashämmarna är effekterna inte stora och slutresultatet är bara en fördröjning av minnesförlusten.

Båda dessa läkemedel finns i generisk form, och det är rimligt att pröva dem och se hur någon svarar på dem.

En sista medicin att nämna kallas lecanemab. Det är en intravenös infusion som riktar sig mot amyloid, en typ av protein som utvecklas i hjärnan hos personer med Alzheimers demens. Medicinen verkar fungera ganska bra för att rensa amyloid från patienternas hjärnor. Denna medicin är mycket dyr (26 500 dollar per år) och har kopplats till en ökning av stroke. I studierna minskades demenssymtomen bara med cirka 30 procent jämfört med placebo.

Det finns inga andra läkemedel för närvarande godkända för att behandla demens.

Terapi utan läkemedel

Det finns flera saker som människor kan göra för att hjälpa till att bromsa utvecklingen av demens. Dessa kan vara hjälpsamma för personer som har en stark familjehistoria av demens och vill förebygga dess uppkomst.

Kardiovaskulär träning är mycket viktigt. Läkare nämner motion i relation till nästan alla kroniska sjukdomar eftersom det visat sig fungera. I fallet demens har personer som motionerar regelbundet ungefär 30 procent sänkt risk att utveckla sjukdomen. Regelbunden träning verkar sakta ner demensens progression.4

Att göra pussel som kräver mental aktivitet, som Sudoku eller korsord, verkar hjälpa till att sakta ner minnesförlustens progression och kan också minska risken att utveckla demens.

Slutligen är det hjälpsamt att lära sig något nytt. Personer som lär sig en ny färdighet eller fokuserar på att lära sig ett nytt språk hjälper sina minnen ganska mycket. En studie jämförde äldre personer som lärde sig en ny färdighet med personer som gick på sociala evenemang.

Poängen verkar vara att våra hjärnor behöver stimuleras för att skapa nya banor, annars tenderar de att brytas ner.5

Att vårda någon med demens

Att vårda någon med demens är utmanande på flera sätt. Det är ofta svårt att veta hur mycket självständighet man ska tillåta personen. Det har skrivits många böcker om detta ämne, men det finns några saker som är värda att nämna.

Det är viktigt att undvika farliga saker. De två farligaste sakerna för någon med bristfälligt minne är att köra bil och att laga mat. Båda dessa verkar vardagliga, och personen kan verka klara det bra, men de kan snabbt bli ett problem.

Risken med att köra bil eller vagn är tvådelad. För det första fryser vissa personer på vissa punkter och minns inte hur man utför en viss färdighet. Detta kan vara ett problem, inte bara för dem utan också för andra i trafiken.

För det andra kan äldre personer ge sig ut på korta resor till en lokal affär eller restaurang och hamna vilse. Jag har haft patienter som hamnat körandes runt i timmar och försökt hitta hem när de blivit förvirrade på väg till stan.

Laga mat handlar förstås om att komma ihåg att ställa timers och ta bort saker från spisen eller ugnen i rätt tid.

Många gånger inser inte personer med demens hur mycket deras förmågor har försämrats och motsätter sig tanken på att ge upp bilnycklarna. Kanske handlar det helt enkelt om förlorad självständighet, men det är svårt att möta faktum att man inte längre är säker bakom ratten.

Försök hålla saker oförändrade i rummet och hemmet. Även små förändringar i möblering kan vara nog för att rubba situationen. Att ta någon ur sitt hem – till exempel att lägga in dem på sjukhus – gör ofta saker mycket värre. Plötsligt blir förvirring som verkade mild tidigare nu extrem.

Om det finns någon frukt av Anden som är avgörande för att hantera någon med demens, är det tålamod. Ingen av oss har så mycket tålamod som behövs; när demens sprider sig blir tålamodet fruktansvärt tunt.

Personer med demens agerar ofta som barn på en lång resa. De frågar om och om igen när de ska åka hem. De undrar var avlidna släktingar är eller varför barnen inte är hemma än. Ingen förklaring hjälper, för bara en minut eller två efter att de ställt frågan har de glömt svaret och frågar igen.

Deras färdigheter fladdrar ofta. Ena dagen kan de knäppa sin skjorta, nästa dag verkar den färdigheten ha flugit ut genom fönstret. Det är lätt att tro att de inte “anstränger sig” och att de skulle kunna göra mer om de bara ansträngde sig.

Tyvärr innebär det faktum att någon med demens kunde göra något igår inte att de kommer ihåg hur man gör det idag. Att bli upprörd på dem förvärrar bara situationen eftersom det tillför ångest till en person som redan saknar minnet av hur man utför en färdighet.

Svara personen så vänligt som möjligt så mycket som möjligt, även om det är femtiofemte gången du svarar samma fråga. Använd också distraktioner. Om det finns en aktivitet som de fortfarande kan göra, som sömnad eller pussel (även barns pussel med riktigt stora bitar), låt dem göra det. Sent i sjukdomen kan det hjälpa att låta dem titta i böcker med vackra bilder eller ibland ge dem en baby-docka att hålla för att lugna dem och avleda deras nuvarande ångest.

Få andra att hjälpa till

Det är lätt att bli frustrerad. Att försöka tillhandahålla all vård själv är ingen långsiktig lösning. Demensvård är ett maraton, inte en sprint. Många lever i åratal efter diagnosen, och även om deras fysiska kropp förblir relativt stark kräver de mer och mer omsorg.

En av välsignelserna med familjeförbindelser och kyrkogemenskap är att vi har människor som kan ställa upp och hjälpa till.

Att låta familjemedlemmar eller vänner rycka in för att ge dig viss avlastning är nyckeln för att inte bli allvarligt utbränd eller till och med arg på någon du bryr dig om. Det är bäst att ta sig tid bort då och då innan du blir mentalt utmattad. Du kanske tror att du klarar dig ganska bra, men vi har alla en tendens att bli trötta i vårt goda görande om vi aldrig får en paus.

Slutsats

Jag önskar att det fanns fler medicinska lösningar för demens. Kanske kommer fler senare. För närvarande är läkemedlen ganska begränsade.

Det viktiga är att omsätta Andens frukt i praktiken. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law” (Galatians 5:22-23).

Även under de mest frustrerande dagarna behöver människor som hanterar svår minnesförlust kärlek, ljuvhet och tålamod från sina familjemedlemmar. Det är endast genom den Helige Andes kraft som vi kan ge den vård som behövs för någon vars kropp är stark, men som inte längre ens känner igen dig.

“It is so hard,” the man sitting across from me said. “We’ve been married for nearly fifty years, but I never expected anything like this.”

“What is going on?” I asked Al, sympathetically.

“It’s Lisa,” he said. “You know her memory has been slipping for a little while. Well, we went to the neurologist like you told us to, and they ordered a whole bunch of tests and a brain scan of some sort. Then, they told her she had dementia.”

“I thought that was what was going on,” I replied.

“I know you told us that,” Al said. “Well, there are times she doesn’t recognize me. She looks at me blankly like she is wondering what crazy stranger has gotten into her house.”

“That’s got to be hard,” I said.

“The only thing I’ve found that brings her back to herself is to go outside and call her on her cell phone. I tell her to come out to the garage, I’ve got something to show her. Somehow when I do that, it brings her back to the present and lets her know who I am – for a little bit, anyway.”

We moved on to talking about other things, but I could tell that Al’s heart was breaking. His wife of 48 years looked the same as ever on the outside and yet, she was a completely different person.

I’d like to explore some of the challenges in dealing with dementia.

Dementia in the Bible

Ecclesiastes 12:1-7 gives a somewhat dismal view of the aging process. “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them; While the sun, or the light, or the moon, or the stars, be not darkened, nor the clouds return after the rain: In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those that look out of the windows be darkened, And the doors shall be shut in the streets, when the sound of the grinding is low, and he shall rise up at the voice of the bird, and all the daughters of musick shall be brought low; Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets: Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern. Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.”

In this passage, the poetic description seems to speak of loss of teeth, loss of hearing, unsteady gait, and general frailty. It is hard to say if any of these images speak of memory loss. What is certain is that the passage begins with a command: “Remember!”

This is not the only place in Scripture where humans are commanded to remember. Over and over, we are told to remember God. We are to make certain that we instruct our children about Him. “And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up” (Deuteronomy 6:7).

The time may come when we are not able to remember anymore. The most important thing – even as we think about the subject of dementia is that we remember the One who made us and follow Him with all our hearts.

What Dementia is

Dementia is any illness that causes a loss of memory, reasoning, and social functioning. Most people think mostly of the loss of memory. I suppose this is because early in the illness other people notice things like difficulty finding words and frequent repetition of stories.

Social functioning is often maintained until late in the illness. If you ask someone with mild dementia if they know today’s date, they will likely answer, “Oh, you know, I stopped paying attention to things like that when I retired.”

The most common cause of dementia is Alzheimer’s dementia – at least 70 percent of people who have progressive memory loss have Alzheimer’s dementia. Alzheimer’s seems to be related to proteins called amyloid, which get deposited in the brain and prevent nerve cells from communicating with each other.

Other causes are vascular dementia, where blockages in the blood vessels in the brain cause the death of nerve cells. Lewy Body Dementia is a sort of memory loss that is associated with Parkinson’s Disease. Approximately eighty percent of people with Parkinson’s Disease will eventually develop dementia.

Diagnosing Dementia

If family members suspect someone is developing memory loss, the best thing is to bring them to their primary care provider for an evaluation. Along with doing a physical exam, the doctor will typically do things like have the patient draw a clock and do a mini mental status exam, which asks the patient to answer a lot of simple questions and do some short-term recall of items.

Blood tests including a thyroid and Vitamin B12 level would be done. A brain scan or ultrasound of the neck arteries might be done as well.

The goal is to identify areas that can be treated and take care of those.

Eliminate Medications

Many medications increase the risk of memory issues. As people get older, trying to avoid these medications is helpful to prevent the development of dementia.

Anticholinergic medications are probably the biggest culprit that I encounter. The most common of these medications are older antihistamines like diphenhydramine (used as either a sleep aid or allergy pill) and doxylamine (used as a sleep aid). In one study, patients who took an anticholinergic medication for the equivalent of three years had a significantly higher risk of dementia than patients who took these sorts of medications for less than three months.1 Older depression medications can also fall into this category.

Anxiety medications, called benzodiazepines, have also been associated with memory issues. Studies indicate that patients who take these medications have a higher risk of developing dementia than patients who do not take them.2

Seizure medications may make thinking ability worse as well. Having a seizure disorder seems to increase the risk of dementia, but certain older medications like valproate and gabapentin seem to make it harder for older people to think clearly, and shifting to lower-risk seizure medications is in order (if possible) for older people.

There are times when someone needs to take medication, but as patients get older, it is important to think about the risks of those medications. There is a list of medications that are wisest to avoid for patients over 65 years of age, called the Beers List. Substituting similar medications with fewer side effects or using lower doses is recommended.3

Medical Treatments

The first rule when dealing with dementia is to make certain that all of the metabolic things are in as good control as possible. So, if someone has diabetes, it is best to make certain that their sugar is in as good control as possible. If someone has high blood pressure, make certain that it is well-regulated (this is particularly true if someone has vascular dementia).

There are several different classes of medications that are approved for treating dementia. One group is the cholinesterase inhibitors. These medications raise the level of a chemical called acetylcholine in the brain and peripheral nervous system. These medications are certainly not miracle drugs and at best they seem to slow the progression of memory loss and do not really restore previous brain function.

The other medication is called memantine. It works by targeting the glutamate receptor in the brain. Just as with the cholinesterase inhibitors, the effects are not huge and the end result only slows the memory loss.

Both of these medications are generic, and it is reasonable to try them and see how someone responds to them.

One last medication to mention is called lecanemab. It is an IV infusion that targets amyloid, a kind of protein that develops in the brain of people with Alzheimer’s dementia. The medication seems to work quite well at clearing amyloid from patient’s brains. This medication is very expensive ($26,500 per year)and it has been linked to an increase in strokes. In the studies, dementia symptoms were only slowed by about 30 percent compared with a placebo.

There are no other medications currently approved to treat dementia.

Non-medication Therapies

There are several things that people can do to help slow the progression of dementia. These can be helpful for people who have a strong family history of dementia and want to prevent its onset.

Cardiovascular exercise is very important. Doctors mention exercise in relation to nearly every chronic illness because it has been shown to work. In the case of dementia, people who exercise regularly have about 30 percent decreased risk of developing the disease. Regular exercise seems to slow the progression of dementia.4

Doing puzzles that require mental activity, like Sudoku or crossword puzzles seems to help slow the progression of memory loss and may also reduce the chance of developing dementia.

Lastly, it is helpful to learn something new. People who learn a new skill or focus on learning a new language help their memories quite a bit. A study compared older people who learned a new skill with people who went to social events.

The point seems to be that our brains need to be pushed to create new pathways or they will tend to break down.5

Caring For Someone with Dementia

Caring for someone with dementia is challenging in a number of ways. It is often difficult to know how much independence to allow the person. There have been many books written on this subject, but there are a few things that are worth mentioning.

It is important to avoid dangerous things. The two most dangerous things for someone with faulty memory are driving and cooking. Both of these seem commonplace, and the person may seem to be doing fine, but they can become a problem very quickly.

The danger of driving a car or a buggy is twofold. First, some people freeze at certain points, not remembering how to do a particular skill. This can be a problem, not only for them but also for others on the road.

Second, older people can start off on short journeys to a local store or restaurant and end up getting lost. I have had patients who ended up driving around for hours trying to find their way home when they got confused driving to town.

Cooking, of course, really comes down to a question of remembering to set timers and take things off the stove or out of the oven at the appropriate time.

Many times, people who have dementia do not realize how much their abilities have slipped and resist the idea that they need to give up the car keys. Maybe it simply comes down to a loss of independence, but it is hard to face the fact that you are no longer safe behind the wheel.

Try to keep things the same within the room and the home. Even small changes in room arrangement can be enough to upset the situation. Taking someone out of their home – for instance, admitting them to the hospital often makes things a lot worse. Suddenly, confusion that only seemed mild before is now extremely high.

If there is a fruit of the spirit that is key for dealing with someone with dementia, it is patience. None of us has as much patience as we need, as dementia spreads that patience awfully thin.

People with dementia often act like children on a long trip. They ask over and over when they are going home. They wonder where dead relatives are or why the children aren’t home yet. No amount of explanation helps, because only a minute or two after they ask the question, they have forgotten the answer and are asking again.

Their skills often wax and wane. One day, they can button their shirt, and the next day, that skill seems to have flown out the window. It is easy to believe that they aren’t “trying hard” and that they could do more if they would only make the effort.

Unfortunately, the fact that someone with dementia could do something yesterday doesn’t mean that they can remember how to do it today. Getting upset with them only makes these things worse as it adds anxiety to a person who already lacks the memory of how to do a skill.

As much as possible, answer the person gently even if it is the fifty-third time that you have answered the same question. Use distractions as well. If there is an activity that they can still do, such as sewing or jigsaw puzzles (even children’s puzzles with really big pieces), get them to do it. Late in the illness, letting them look at books with pretty pictures or sometimes even giving them a baby doll to hold can help settle them and distract them from their anxieties of the moment.

Get Others to Help

It is easy to become frustrated. Trying to provide all of the care needed by yourself is not a long-term solution. Dementia care is a marathon and not a sprint. Many people live for years after the diagnosis, and even though their physical body remains relatively strong, they require more and more care.

One of the blessings of having family connections and church communities is that we have people who are available to provide assistance.

Having family members or friends step in to give you some respite is key to not becoming seriously burned out or even angry with someone that you care about. It is best to take some time away periodically before you are mentally depleted. You may think you are doing fairly well, but all of us have a tendency to get weary in well doing if we never get a break.

Conclusion

I wish there were more medical solutions for dementia. Perhaps more will come later. For now, medications are quite limited.

The key is to put the fruit of the Spirit into practice. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law” (Galatians 5:22-23).

Even on the most frustrating days, people who are dealing with severe memory loss need love, gentleness, and patience from their family members. It is only through the Holy Spirit’s power that we can provide the care that is needed for someone whose body is strong, but who no longer even recognizes you.

«Det er så vanskelig,» sa mannen som satt overfor meg. «Vi har vært gift i nesten femti år, men jeg hadde aldri forventet noe slikt.»

«Hva skjer?» spurte jeg Al medfølende.

«Det er Lisa,» sa han. «Du vet at hukommelsen hennes har sklidd litt den siste tiden. Vel, vi dro til nevrologen som du sa, og de bestilte en rekke tester og en slags hjerneskanning. Så sa de at hun hadde demens.»

«Jeg trodde det var det som foregikk,» svarte jeg.

«Jeg vet du sa det,» sa Al. «Vel, det er tider hun ikke kjenner meg igjen. Hun ser på meg tomt som om hun lurer på hvilken gal fremmed som har kommet inn i huset hennes.»

«Det må være vanskelig,» sa jeg.

«Det eneste jeg har funnet som får henne tilbake til seg selv, er å gå ut og ringe henne på mobiltelefonen. Jeg sier at hun skal komme ut i garasjen, jeg har noe å vise henne. På en eller annen måte når jeg gjør det, får det henne tilbake til nåtiden og lar henne vite hvem jeg er – for en liten stund, i alle fall.»

Vi gikk videre til å snakke om andre ting, men jeg kunne se at Als hjerte brast. Hans kone gjennom 48 år så ut som vanlig på utsiden, og likevel var hun en helt annen person.

Jeg vil gjerne utforske noen av utfordringene ved å håndtere demens.

Dementia in the Bible

Ecclesiastes 12:1-7 gives a somewhat dismal view of the aging process. “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them; While the sun, or the light, or the moon, or the stars, be not darkened, nor the clouds return after the rain: In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those that look out of the windows be darkened, And the doors shall be shut in the streets, when the sound of the grinding is low, and he shall rise up at the voice of the bird, and all the daughters of musick shall be brought low; Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets: Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern. Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.”

I dette avsnittet ser den poetiske beskrivelsen ut til å tale om tap av tenner, tap av hørsel, ustø gange og generell skrøpelighet. Det er vanskelig å si om noen av disse bildene beskriver hukommelsestap. Det som er sikkert, er at avsnittet begynner med et bud: «Husk!»

Dette er ikke det eneste stedet i Skriften hvor mennesker får befalingen om å huske. Gang på gang blir vi fortalt å huske Gud. Vi skal sørge for å lære barna våre om Ham. «And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up» (Deuteronomy 6:7).

Tiden kan komme når vi ikke er i stand til å huske lenger. Det viktigste – selv når vi tenker på demens – er at vi husker Den som skapte oss og følger Ham av hele vårt hjerte.

What Dementia is

Demens er enhver sykdom som forårsaker tap av hukommelse, resonnement og sosial fungering. De fleste tenker først og fremst på hukommelsestap. Jeg antar at dette er fordi andre tidlig i sykdomsforløpet legger merke til ting som vanskeligheter med å finne ord og hyppig repetisjon av historier.

Sosial fungering opprettholdes ofte til sykdommen er langt kommet. Hvis du spør noen med mild demens om dagens dato, vil de sannsynligvis svare: «Å, du vet, jeg sluttet å følge med på slike ting da jeg pensjonerte meg.»

Den vanligste årsaken til demens er Alzheimers demens – minst 70 prosent av de som har progressivt hukommelsestap har Alzheimers. Alzheimer virker å være relatert til proteiner kalt amyloid, som avsettes i hjernen og hindrer nerveceller i å kommunisere med hverandre.

Andre årsaker er vaskulær demens, der blokkeringer i blodårene i hjernen forårsaker død av nerveceller. Lewy body-demens er en type hukommelsestap som er assosiert med Parkinsons sykdom. Omtrent åtti prosent av personer med Parkinsons sykdom vil etter hvert utvikle demens.

Diagnosing Dementia

Hvis familiemedlemmer mistenker at noen utvikler hukommelsestap, er det beste å ta dem med til fastlegen for en vurdering. I tillegg til en fysisk undersøkelse vil legen vanligvis be pasienten tegne en klokke og gjøre en kort mental status-undersøkelse, som ber pasienten svare på mange enkle spørsmål og gjøre noen korttidsgjenkallinger.

Blodprøver, inkludert skjoldbruskkjertel- og vitamin B12-nivå, vil bli tatt. En hjerneskanning eller ultralyd av halspulsårene kan også bli utført.

Målet er å identifisere områder som kan behandles og ta seg av dem.

Eliminate Medications

Mange medisiner øker risikoen for hukommelsesproblemer. Etter hvert som folk blir eldre, er det nyttig å prøve å unngå disse medisinene for å forebygge utvikling av demens.

Antikolinerge medisiner er sannsynligvis den største synderen jeg møter. De vanligste av disse medisinene er eldre antihistaminer som difenhydramin (brukes enten som sovemiddel eller allergipille) og doksylamin (brukes som sovemiddel). I en studie hadde pasienter som tok en antikolinerg medisin tilsvarende tre års bruk en betydelig høyere risiko for demens enn pasienter som tok slike medisiner i mindre enn tre måneder.1 Eldre antidepressiva kan også falle inn i denne kategorien.

Angstmedisiner, kalt benzodiazepiner, har også vært assosiert med hukommelsesproblemer. Studier indikerer at pasienter som tar disse medisinene har høyere risiko for å utvikle demens enn pasienter som ikke tar dem.2

Anfallspreparater kan også gjøre tankeevnen dårligere. Å ha en anfallslidelse ser ut til å øke risikoen for demens, men visse eldre medisiner som valproat og gabapentin ser ut til å gjøre det vanskeligere for eldre å tenke klart, og det kan være nødvendig å bytte til lavrisikomedisiner mot anfall (hvis mulig) for eldre.

Det finnes tider hvor noen trenger å ta medisin, men etter hvert som pasientene blir eldre, er det viktig å tenke på risikoene ved disse medisinene. Det finnes en liste over medisiner som det er klokt å unngå for pasienter over 65 år, kalt Beers-listen. Å erstatte med lignende medisiner med færre bivirkninger eller å bruke lavere doser anbefales.3

Medical Treatments

Den første regelen ved håndtering av demens er å sørge for at alle metabolske forhold er så godt kontrollert som mulig. Så hvis noen har diabetes, er det best å sørge for at blodsukkeret er så godt kontrollert som mulig. Hvis noen har høyt blodtrykk, må det være godt regulert (dette gjelder særlig ved vaskulær demens).

Det finnes flere ulike grupper medikamenter som er godkjent for å behandle demens. En gruppe er kolinesterasehemmere. Disse medisinene øker nivået av et kjemisk stoff kalt acetylkolin i hjernen og det perifere nervesystemet. Disse medisinene er absolutt ikke mirakelmidler og på det beste ser de ut til å bremse utviklingen av hukommelsestap og gjenoppretter ikke tidligere hjernefunksjon.

Den andre medisinen kalles memantin. Den virker ved å målrette glutamatreseptoren i hjernen. Akkurat som med kolinesterasehemmerne er effektene ikke store og sluttresultatet er bare en nedbremsing av hukommelsestapet.

Begge disse medisinene finnes som generika, og det er rimelig å prøve dem og se hvordan noen responderer.

En siste medisin å nevne heter lecanemab. Det er en intravenøs infusjon som retter seg mot amyloid, en type protein som utvikler seg i hjernen hos personer med Alzheimers demens. Medisinen ser ut til å fungere ganske godt ved å fjerne amyloid fra pasienters hjerner. Denne medisinen er svært dyr ($26,500 per år) og den har vært knyttet til en økning i slag. I studiene ble demenssymptomene bare bremset med omtrent 30 prosent sammenlignet med placebo.

Det finnes for øyeblikket ingen andre medisiner godkjent for å behandle demens.

Non-medication Therapies

Det er flere ting folk kan gjøre for å hjelpe med å bremse utviklingen av demens. Disse kan være nyttige for personer som har sterk familiehistorie med demens og ønsker å forebygge utbrudd.

Kardiovaskulær trening er svært viktig. Leger nevner trening i forbindelse med nesten alle kroniske sykdommer fordi det har vist seg å virke. Når det gjelder demens, har folk som trener regelmessig omtrent 30 prosent redusert risiko for å utvikle sykdommen. Regelmessig trening ser også ut til å bremse sykdomsforløpet.4

Å gjøre puslespill som krever mental aktivitet, som Sudoku eller kryssord, ser ut til å hjelpe med å bremse utviklingen av hukommelsestap og kan også redusere sjansen for å utvikle demens.

Til slutt er det nyttig å lære noe nytt. Personer som lærer en ny ferdighet eller fokuserer på å lære et nytt språk hjelper hukommelsen sin betydelig. En studie sammenlignet eldre som lærte en ny ferdighet med folk som dro på sosiale arrangementer.

Poenget ser ut til å være at hjernen vår må presses til å skape nye baner, ellers vil de ha en tendens til å bryte ned.5

Caring For Someone with Dementia

Omsorg for noen med demens er utfordrende på flere måter. Det er ofte vanskelig å vite hvor mye selvstendighet man skal tillate personen. Det finnes mange bøker skrevet om dette emnet, men det er noen få ting verdt å nevne.

Det er viktig å unngå farlige ting. De to farligste aktivitetene for noen med svekket hukommelse er kjøring og matlaging. Begge kan virke hverdagslige, og personen kan synes å klare seg fint, men de kan raskt bli et problem.

Faren ved å kjøre bil eller vogn er todelt. For det første kan noen fryse ved bestemte punkter og ikke huske hvordan man utfører en bestemt ferdighet. Dette kan være et problem, ikke bare for dem, men også for andre i trafikken.

For det andre kan eldre starte på korte turer til en lokal butikk eller restaurant og ende opp med å gå seg vill. Jeg har hatt pasienter som kjørte rundt i flere timer og prøvde å finne veien hjem når de ble forvirret på vei til byen.

Matlaging handler selvsagt om å huske å sette tidtakere og ta ting av komfyren eller ut av ovnen til riktig tid.

Mange ganger innser ikke personer med demens hvor mye evnene deres har sviktet og motsetter seg ideen om å gi fra seg bilnøklene. Kanskje handler det rett og slett om tap av uavhengighet, men det er vanskelig å innrømme at man ikke lenger er trygg bak rattet.

Prøv å holde ting like i rommet og hjemmet. Selv små endringer i møblering kan være nok til å forstyrre situasjonen. Å ta noen ut av hjemmet deres – for eksempel å legge dem inn på sykehus – gjør ofte ting mye verre. Plutselig blir en forvirring som tidligere virket mild, nå svært uttalt.

Hvis det finnes en åndens frukt som er nøkkelen for å håndtere noen med demens, er det tålmodighet. Ingen av oss har så mye tålmodighet som vi trenger; når demens sprer seg blir tålmodigheten virkelig tynn.

Personer med demens oppfører seg ofte som barn på en lang reise. De spør om og om igjen når de skal hjem. De lurer på hvor døde slektninger er eller hvorfor barna ikke er hjemme ennå. Ingen forklaring hjelper, for bare et minutt eller to etter at de stiller spørsmålet, har de glemt svaret og spør igjen.

Ferdighetene deres kommer ofte og går. En dag kan de kneppe skjorten, og neste dag ser det ut som om ferdigheten er forsvunnet. Det er lett å tro at de ikke «prøver hardt» og at de kunne gjøre mer hvis de bare anstrengte seg.

Dessverre betyr det faktum at noen med demens kunne gjøre noe i går ikke at de husker hvordan i dag. Å bli sint på dem gjør bare situasjonen verre fordi det tilfører angst til en person som allerede mangler hukommelsen for hvordan man utfører en ferdighet.

Så langt det lar seg gjøre, svar personen mildt selv om det er den femtitrende gangen du svarer på samme spørsmål. Bruk også distraksjon. Hvis det finnes en aktivitet de fortsatt kan gjøre, som å sy eller pusle (selv barnas puslespill med veldig store brikker), få dem til å gjøre det. Sent i sykdomsforløpet kan det å la dem se i bøker med fine bilder eller noen ganger gi dem en dukke å holde hjelpe med å roe dem og avlede dem fra øyeblikkets angst.

Get Others to Help

Det er lett å bli frustrert. Å prøve å gi all omsorg selv er ikke en langsiktig løsning. Demensomsorg er et maraton, ikke en sprint. Mange lever i år etter diagnosen, og selv om kroppen forblir relativt sterk, trenger de mer og mer omsorg.

En av velsignelsene ved å ha familietilknytninger og kirkesamfunn er at vi har mennesker som er tilgjengelige til å gi hjelp.

At familiemedlemmer eller venner trår inn for å gi deg litt avlastning er avgjørende for ikke å bli alvorlig utbrent eller til og med sint på noen du bryr deg om. Det er best å ta seg tid borte med jevne mellomrom før du er mentalt utslitt. Du tror kanskje du klarer deg greit, men alle av oss har en tendens til å bli trette i velgjørenhet hvis vi aldri får en pause.

Conclusion

Jeg skulle ønske det fantes flere medisinske løsninger for demens. Kanskje kommer det flere senere. Foreløpig er medikamentene ganske begrensede.

Nøkkelen er å sette åndens frukt ut i livet. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law” (Galatians 5:22-23).

Selv på de mest frustrerende dagene trenger mennesker som har alvorlig hukommelsestap kjærlighet, mildhet og tålmodighet fra sine familiemedlemmer. Det er bare ved Den Hellige Ånds kraft at vi kan gi den omsorgen som trengs for en som har en sterk kropp, men som ikke engang lenger kjenner deg igjen.

“Adrianna, what’s the temperature outside?” asked Asher. He and Adrianna were sitting at the table doing school with their siblings Emily and Kianna.

“Probably about 50.” Adrianna glanced lazily at the thermometer. “Hey, it’s 65 degrees! Mom, may we eat lunch outside?”

Mom looked up from the sink. “If you do a good job with your school until then, you may,” she told them. “And if you get your school done before lunch, you may play outside for a while this afternoon.”

Asher let out a whoop and started writing fast. The girls grinned at each other and picked up their pencils.

Everyone worked diligently until lunchtime. Then Adrianna made sandwiches while Asher put cookies in bags, Emily collected bags of chips, and Kianna ran down to the basement to grab a few apples. They each packed their lunch in a shopping bag and went out to their picnic spot, a big, flat rock in a clearing in the woods.

They ate quickly, then Adrianna suggested, “Let’s go kayak on the pond!”

“I guess we could,” said Asher slowly. “But didn’t Mom say that Emily and Kianna are too small to handle the kayaks?”

“Oh, yes, I guess she did. Well, they can play on the swings or something,” she shrugged

“I think we should play something everyone can help with,” said Asher. He turned to Emily and Kianna. “What do you want to do?”

“Let’s make a playhouse!” suggested Kianna.

“Yes, let’s!” Emily agreed. “You could hunt for us,” she told Asher.

“And Adrianna could be the mom!” said Kianna.

Adrianna stood with a scowl on her face. Playhouse indeed! She was way too old for that! “I’m going kayaking,” she announced. “You can just have your playhouse.” She picked up her shopping bag and put her sandwich and cookie bags into it. She threw her apple core to the dogs and started for the house.

“Adrianna, can you please take ours too?” begged Emily. “You're going to the house anyway.”

“You can take care of your own stuff,” Adrianna called back, crossly. She dropped her shopping bag on the counter, hoping to slip out of the house before Mom saw her.

She heard her mom’s voice. “Wait, Adrianna, what’s wrong? Your face looks like a thunderstorm!”

Adrianna sighed. She hadn’t been fast enough. “I wanted to go kayaking, but Asher doesn’t want to,” she grumbled.

“Well,” said Mom slowly, “I think Asher is remembering that the other girls can't handle kayaks yet. What are they doing?”

“They’re building a playhouse. I'm way too old for that!” Adrianna burst out.

Mom smiled, “What makes you think that?”

“I'm sure none of the girls my age do stuff like that with their little siblings.”

“Are you sure you're not being selfish?” Mom asked. “Sometimes, we need to give up what we want so that others can be happy.”

Adrianna shrugged and went out to the shed to get a kayak. She lifted her blue kayak off the rack and hauled it down to the pond. She snapped the paddle together, hopped into the seat, and pushed the kayak onto the smooth surface of the water. She sighed with pleasure. This was way better than building a playhouse in the woods! She took a few loops around the pond before her paddle began to slow. Somehow it wasn’t as fun this time. She heard Asher and the girls laughing and shouting as they played. Maybe Mom was right, she thought. Maybe I would be happier if I gave up what I want so that we can all play together. Slowly she paddled to the edge of the pond. She stepped out of the kayak, pulled it out of the water, and flipped it over to dry. Resolutely, she walked out of the pasture to find Asher and the girls.

“Hey! Here comes Adrianna!” called Emily happily as Adrianna walked up.

Adrianna grinned, “It looks like you have your house about set up,” she said encouragingly. “What do you need to finish it?”

“We still need a stove, and something for a countertop,” said Kianna.

“I can help you find something,” Adrianna told them. Together they hunted in the woods and the shed for boards and logs to finish the house. When suppertime came and they went in for supper, Adrianna was very happy. Mom was right, she thought. It is more fun to give up my way and do what everyone else wants to.

“شاید پچاس کے قریب۔” ایڈریانا نے آہستگی سے تھرمامیٹر کی طرف دیکھا۔ “اوہ، یہ پینسٹھ ڈگری ہے! امی، کیا ہم باہر دوپہر کا کھانا کھا سکتے ہیں؟”

امی نے سنک سے نظریں اٹھائیں۔ “اگر تم اس وقت تک اپنا اسکول اچھے سے کر لو تو ہاں،” انہوں نے کہا۔ “اور اگر تم دوپہر سے پہلے اپنا اسکول ختم کر لو تو دوپہر کو تھوڑی دیر باہر کھیل بھی سکتے ہو۔”

آشر نے خوشی سے چیخ ماری اور تیزی سے لکھنے لگا۔ لڑکیاں ایک دوسرے کو مسکرا کر دیکھیں اور اپنے پنسل اٹھا لیں۔

سب نے دوپہر کے کھانے تک محنت سے کام کیا۔ پھر ایڈریانا نے سینڈوچ بنائے جبکہ آشر نے کوکیز تھیلوں میں رکھیں، ایمیلی نے چپس کے تھیلے اکٹھے کیے، اور کیانا تہ خانے کی طرف دوڑی تاکہ کچھ سیب لے آئے۔ انہوں نے ہر ایک نے اپنا لنچ ایک شاپنگ بیگ میں رکھا اور جنگل کی ایک صفائی میں پڑے بڑے، ہموار پتھر کے پاس اپنی پکنک جگہ کی طرف گئے۔

انہوں نے تیزی سے کھایا، پھر ایڈریانا نے تجویز دی، “چلو تالاب میں کیاکنگ کرتے ہیں!”

“شاید ہم کر سکتے ہیں،” آشر نے آہستگی سے کہا۔ “لیکن امی نے تو کہا تھا کہ ایمیلی اور کیانا ابھی کیاک سنبھالنے کے لائق نہیں ہیں؟”

“اوہ ہاں، شاید انہوں نے کہا تھا۔ خیر، وہ جھولوں یا کچھ اور پر کھیل سکتی ہیں،” وہ کندھے اچکاتے ہوئے بولی۔

“میرے خیال میں ہمیں ایسا کھیل کھیلنا چاہیے جس میں سب مدد کر سکیں،” آشر نے کہا۔ وہ ایمیلی اور کیانا کی طرف مڑا۔ “تم دونوں کیا کرنا چاہتی ہو؟”

“چلو ایک پلے ہاؤس بناتے ہیں!” کیانا نے تجویز پیش کی۔

“ہاں، چلو!” ایمیلی نے اتفاق کیا۔ “تم ہمارے لیے چیزیں ڈھونڈ سکتے ہو،” اس نے آشر سے کہا۔

“اور ایڈریانا ماں بن سکتی ہے!” کیانا نے کہا۔

ایڈریانا نے چہرے پر خفا پن سجائے کھڑے ہو کر دیکھا۔ پلے ہاؤس! وہ اس کے لیے بہت بڑی تھی! “میں کیاکنگ کرنے جا رہی ہوں،” اس نے اعلان کیا۔ “تم لوگ اپنا پلے ہاؤس خود ہی بنا لو۔” اس نے اپنا شاپنگ بیگ اٹھایا اور اپنے سینڈوچ اور کوکی کے تھیلے اس میں ڈال دیے۔ اس نے اپنی سیب کی چھلی کتوں کو پھینک دی اور گھر کی جانب چل پڑی۔

“ایڈریانا، کیا تم براہِ مہربانی ہمارے لیے بھی لے جا سکتی ہو؟” ایمیلی نے التجا کی۔ “تم تو ویسے بھی گھر جا رہی ہو۔”

“اپنے سامان کا خیال تم خود رکھ سکتے ہو،” ایڈریانا نے غصے سے پکارا۔ وہ اپنا شاپنگ بیگ کاؤنٹر پر گرایا، امید کرتے ہوئے کہ امی اسے دیکھنے سے پہلے وہ گھر سے نکل نکل جائے گی۔

ایڈریانا نے آہ بھری۔ وہ اتنی تیز نہیں تھی۔ “میں کیاکنگ کرنا چاہتی تھی، مگر آشر نہیں چاہتا،” اس نے غرارت سے کہا۔

“اچھا،” امی نے آہستگی سے کہا، “میں سمجھتی ہوں آشر یہ یاد کر رہا ہے کہ وہ دوسری لڑکیاں ابھی کیاک سنبھال نہیں سکتیں۔ وہ لوگ کیا کر رہے ہیں؟”

“مجھے یقین ہے کہ میری عمر کی کوئی لڑکیاں اپنے چھوٹے بہن بھائیوں کے ساتھ ایسی چیزیں نہیں کرتی ہیں۔”

“کیا تمہیں یقین ہے کہ تم خود غرض تو نہیں ہو رہی؟” امی نے پوچھا۔ “کبھی کبھی، ہمیں اپنی خواہشات چھوڑنی پڑتی ہیں تاکہ دوسروں کو خوشی ملے۔”

“ہائے! ایڈریانا آ رہی ہے!” ایمیلی نے خوشی سے پکارا جب ایڈریانا پاس آئی۔

“ہمیں ابھی ایک چولہا چاہیے، اور کاؤنٹر ٹاپ کے لیے کچھ چاہیے،” کیانا نے کہا۔

“Get out of my shop! I don’t need people like you around me! And never come back!” My lips quivered as I looked into the dark, angry eyes of the yelling man. I blinked back the unbidden tears, realizing that once more, I had to leave this man that I loved. All night I could sense that we were coming to this, and I had tried so hard not to let it happen. With one last attempt, I feebly yelled above the tension, “Ken, we don’t want to ...” but once more, I was rudely cut off. With slumped shoulders and downcast eyes, I turned to escape the confines of his dingy, pawn shop, his ever-crescendoing voice drowning the last hope of respite.

The lingering smell of smoke and the echo of his angry voice joined the troubled thoughts of my emotionally overwrought mind, as I slowly walked up the street. “What do you think, Josh?” I asked my faithful, quiet friend.

“I don’t know, " he responded, and we fell back into silent anguish at the outcome of our supposed Bible study, grasping for an explanation for the terrible response. What could we have done differently? Why could he not accept the truth? What lay behind those flashing eyes, and what memories are stored beneath his ever-crowning beanie?

Ken was born on a country farm in the rolling hills of Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, a splendid place for a curious and adventurous little boy to live.

When Ken was four years old, his parents separated. He had heard them fighting a lot, but he didn’t know that it was possible for Mom and Dad to separate. It crushed his heart and confused his innocent soul. He did not know how to handle the stress and change that was tossed on his peaceful life.

The terror and confusion of his mom hurriedly packing their belongings, loading him and his siblings in the car, and driving away are still riveted in his mind. It made no sense! Why couldn’t they just go home? In his musty bedroom at their little, dingy apartment, he lay staring at the moldy ceiling, wondering endlessly what had gone so wrong.

Ken soon adjusted to his new home in the city of Pottsville with only cars, people, and sidewalks instead of cows, frogs, and mud. But fate did not leave the small security his new lifestyle provided him. His mom was not able to properly care for him and his siblings, and so the children were placed in different foster homes. That was even worse than leaving Dad! The clothes he wore were the only things familiar to him. Instead of understanding and loving him, each new family brought more yelling, hatred, and beating. Terror, tears, loneliness, and pain accompanied him.

Ken thought the second foster home that he was placed in would be a safe, loving home. The dad was tall and strong and appeared to be gentle. The mom was overweight, but her friendly smile resolved his fears. But the first night, when he reached for the food, he accidentally dumped a cup of water. She screamed at him and told him that he was worthless, and she wished they had never gotten him. The dad continued eating as if he didn't hear or care. Why didn’t the strong man stop her?

That evening, Ken crawled into his big, strange bed, already crying in loneliness, when he heard the mom yell. He quickly jumped out of bed and, with trembling legs, slipped behind the door to hide. She charged up the stairs bellowing angrily, and Ken was sure that he was in trouble. To his relief, she continued down the hall. He was still too scared to leave his hiding place for fear of receiving a beating. He wiped his tears as he began to sing under his breath a song he had heard in Sunday school, “Jesus loves the little children, all the children of the world.” He stopped to think, and his crying quit. “Then why am I here? " he wondered. “Have I done something wrong? God must not love little children. That song is not true! If God loved me I would not be here!" With that conclusion, he burst into tears and lost hope in God. He woke the next morning, still hidden behind the door.

Darkness had long fallen, and my family was all peacefully sleeping in our old farmhouse. I cried myself to sleep, crying for Ken's soul, crying because I didn’t know what to do, crying because my friend, the man I longed to see at peace with God, hated me.

Ken continued to fire questions. “How can God be good and allow so much bad? How could God let children suffer?” I listened on as he continued saying the same things that I heard so many times before, giving me no chance to talk.

Again, it was time to leave, and I was so glad to do so. He kept talking as we backed out the door. Once more, my friend and I walked up the street —tired, frustrated, and wishing never to come back.

Ken was 13 years old, and his life was no better than it had been when he was first put into the foster system. His life was in turmoil. He was continually yelled at and belittled at home. Ken was tired of crying. No one cared, and there was no one with whom he could share his problem. That’s when he came up with his clever plan. His school friend was a hippie, and his parents traveled a lot. They were called Gypsies. He heard that they were headed to California. So, Ken told them about his terrible life and asked if they would give him a ride. They were glad to help.

That exciting morning, he just did his usual thing. He left for school and instead went to California. He didn’t mind leaving all his stuff behind—he really didn’t have much anyway. His foster parents didn’t even care that he left.

In California, Ken lived on the beach and worked for fishermen, and whoever else needed help. He always had enough to eat and something to do. He had his fellow beach bums, but he was still alone inside. His heart was still empty. He longed for love.

Ken lived on the beach for a year and a half and then hitchhiked to Arizona. There he found a home in a homeless shelter and got a job. He did well and soon was on his own, but his search for love took him down the wrong roads. Ken really wanted to be married to a loving wife and have a family, but the girl he married did not marry him because of love. She was hurt, and Ken’s own hurt soul was attracted to her. They got married and all was well for a few years until he found out that his wife was seeing other men. His heart was broken, and his world was thrown into turmoil. Ken wanted desperately to provide security for the children that were born to them, and so he tried his best to stay together. He did not want to put his children through the life that he experienced. But after eight rough years, they got a divorce.

Ken moved on and tried to recover from the devastation of the divorce. His search for love brought him only more sadness and pain. Since Ken was hurt and unhappy, he found satisfaction in making others happy. He spent all his money on them, and when he had nothing more to offer, they left.

Now Ken is sitting in his pawn shop, alone, hurt, sad, and hiding. He found through his sad life that no one cared. Every time that he opened himself to love, he was always hurt. Deep down inside, he truly felt that God did not care. He lost hope in God, people, and last of all, he lost hope in love itself. That is why we were still visiting the dingy, smoke-stained shop after six years of very little apparent success. God kept bringing us back. He put in us a persistent love and relentless burden for this wounded soul. That is why we spent many hours hearing the same criticisms over and over. The same problems, the same confusion.

Nearly every month, he would fluctuate between hope and despair, love and hate, new life in God, and sadness and sin. We never knew what the next visit would bring. We could be swelling with hope and filled with blessing, or torn with angry words and sickened with dread. But we kept going back, and slowly he emerged from the pit of despair, and slowly allowed himself to be wrapped in the wonderful love of God and the glorious message of His redeeming grace. It was amazing to see the change in his life and to hear his ever-growing confidence in the love of Christ.

Today Ken loves the Lord. He is learning to walk with God. He has seen the love of God. He has found hope in God. He has experienced the unconditional love of God. He is still growing, and we are excited to see what God has for him.

I’m so glad that God brought Ken into my life. God had a plan for Ken and I. God wanted to show Ken that He loved him and that He would be there for him even when Josh turned his back on Him. God also wanted me to carry a burden in my youth. He knew how easily I would be distracted with money and fun. He knew that I needed a burden to carry, a soul to care for. He wanted me to be able to see beneath the shell of a hard soul and see a hurting child within. He wanted to give me a burden too big for me to carry so that I would learn to lean on Him. And most of all, He wanted to equip me to serve Him in broader ways.

Fellow Christians, open your lives to the work of God. Find an opportunity to love a hurting soul. Search out someone who needs a friend and love them, and wait and see what God has in store for you. Love until it hurts so badly that you don’t know what to do, and then turn to Jesus, who is there to help you through. God may be waiting for you to make the first step before He will use you. Your life is before you. You can choose to live a comfortable, happy life, or you can open yourself up to be hurt and find that after years pass, your life is overflowing with meaning and purpose. Jesus opened Himself to the pain and anguish of this world, and only through that do we have hope. He is asking us to follow His example, to open ourselves to pain so that others can have hope. And as He was glorified, so will we be glorified, in some measure, someday, and we will never regret the pain that we faced.
